reports.title: Bill Taylor: A life devoted to bass fishing and the people in it
reports.text:
Major League Fishing and the entire bass fishing community are mourning the loss of longtime tournament director, mentor and friend Bill Taylor, who passed away Friday at the age of 79 following a brief battle with liver cancer.
For more than three decades, Bill was one of the most familiar and respected figures in tournament bass fishing. From the early days of Operation Bass through the growth of FLW and eventually MLF, he helped shape how tournaments were operated and how generations of anglers experienced the sport.
He was demanding and meticulous because he cared about getting things right, especially when it came to protecting the integrity of competition. Whether interacting with…

reports.title: Ark Gravity AVID BFS Reel Review: A Serious BFS Performer Without the Premium Price
reports.text:
I’ve spent a lot of time fishing bait finesse system (BFS) gear over the past several years, and one of the things I’ve learned is that a good BFS reel needs to do more than simply cast lightweight lures. It needs to be easy to dial in, balance well with a lightweight rod, and capable of handling everything from tiny lures to the surprisingly big bass that eat them.
The ARK Gravity Avid BFS gets all that done. I’ve been fishing it paired with the FishUSA Flagship BFS Casting Rod, and the combination has worked quite well for me. reports.title: Why the 4/0 EWG Just Might Be the Best Bass Hook of All Time
reports.text:
You can find countless hook brands and styles on the market now. But, in my opinion, none are as versatile as the Gamakatsu EWG (Extra Wide Gap). This hook has dozens of applications in the bass fishing space, from rigging soft plastics to its incorporation into swing heads and even some skirted baits.
Aptly named for its defining characteristic — the extra-wide gap — this hook not only maximizes your hookup ratio, but also holds up to large and small fish alike. If I had to single out the best bass hook of all time, I would have to go with the 4/0 EWG. Here’s why.

reports.text:
With the leaves changing color and Indian Summer all but completed, some states have come to terms with the cold weather. Our office in Minnesota, not far from Leech Lake, likely experienced its last day in the 80s in early October. And now the chill has set in.

reports.title: Researchers Sank 140 Trees in a Lake, and Fish Production Doubled
reports.text:
To get more fish in a lake, just add some trees.
That’s the somewhat simplified conclusion of researchers who added 140 “fish sticks” — fallen or cut-down trees — to northern Wisconsin’s 92-acre Sanford Lake. The goal was to see if additional trees either attract fish already in the lake or lead to more of them.
“ In our project, we found that adding trees doubled the number of fish that Sanford Lake can now support,” says Greg Sass, head of the Wisconsin DNR research team.
In other words, add more trees and higher numbers of fish will eventually follow.

reports.title: Hit Lake Murray’s brush for fall crappie
reports.text:
Don’t miss the fall crappie bite
A s Lake Murray’s water temperature cools down in October, Capt. Brad Taylor of Taylor Outdoors said the crappie fishing gets cranked up.
“October is a great month because you can catch crappie in a number of ways, really just about any way you want to catch them will work,” he said.
One way Taylor targets them this time of year is by fishing brush in the main river channel.
“Fall is kind of a magical time of year for Lake Murray because the shad start working up the river,” he said. “And the crappie follow the bait. If you can find the bait, which isn’t too difficult using electronics, then you can find the crappie.”

reports.text:
Find the bait, find the crappie
S hane Walser of Yadkin Lakes Crappie Guides (336-978-3737) loves fishing High Rock Lake in October.
“It’s a great time to fish, for numerous reasons. The weather is ideal, the summer lake crowds are gone, and the crappie really pick up the bite with the falling temperatures,” he said.
Electronics play a big role in his fishing this month.

reports.title: Yeopim Creek Fliers with Carolina ALL OUT
reports.text:
Fliers are among the most unique panfish in the Carolinas
T he Carolinas are full of numerous species of panfish, and for their size, they all fight like champs. They’re also very tasty. Fliers, although they are found throughout the southeast, are among the least widely distributed panfish, mostly living in swampy, acidic blackwater creeks with low pH.
Where you’ll find fliers, you can always count on finding other panfish as well. They overlap with crappie, bluegill, redbreast and shellcrackers, among other species.
